quizzes.title: Checkpoint 1 — Why Types, Basics, and Functions
quizzes.intro: Check whether you understand TypeScript’s role, core annotations, and typed functions before objects and unions.

questions.prompt: What does TypeScript primarily add on top of JavaScript?

options.text: A brand-new browser runtime that replaces JavaScript engines
A static type system and compiler checks that erase types when emitting JavaScript
Automatic unit tests for every function
A requirement that all variables must be global

questions.explanation: TypeScript checks types at compile time and emits ordinary JavaScript with types erased.

wrongExplanations.a: Browsers and Node still run JavaScript; TypeScript compiles down to JS.
wrongExplanations.c: Types help correctness but do not generate a full test suite.
wrongExplanations.d: TypeScript does not force globals; modular scoped code remains best practice.

questions.prompt: Why is any usually a poor default for beginners?

options.text: Because any makes the compiler slower forever in every project
Because any turns off useful checking for that value, removing much of TypeScript’s benefit
Because any is illegal syntax in modern TypeScript
Because any only works inside interfaces

questions.explanation: any disables type checking for that value, which undermines the safety you adopted TypeScript for.

wrongExplanations.a: The main issue is lost safety, not a universal permanent slowdown claim.
wrongExplanations.c: any is legal; it is just often unwise as a default.
wrongExplanations.d: any can appear in many positions, which is part of the risk.

questions.prompt: Which habit matches “annotate boundaries, infer interiors”?

options.text: Annotate every local variable and never annotate function parameters
Type function inputs and important exported contracts, and let local inference stay clear where obvious
Never write type annotations at all
Only annotate comments, not code

questions.explanation: Boundaries such as parameters and exported APIs benefit most from explicit types; locals can often be inferred.

wrongExplanations.a: That reverses the guidance and often adds noise.
wrongExplanations.c: Skipping annotations entirely weakens contracts at module edges.
wrongExplanations.d: Comments are not a substitute for the type system.

questions.prompt: In function add(a: number, b: number): number, what is the : number after the parameter list?

options.text: A required runtime cast performed by the browser
The declared return type of the function
A label for the first parameter only
Syntax that disables inference project-wide

questions.explanation: The annotation after the parameter list documents and checks the function’s return type.

wrongExplanations.a: Type annotations are compile-time, not browser runtime casts.
wrongExplanations.c: Parameter types appear beside each parameter, not after the whole list.
wrongExplanations.d: A return annotation does not disable project-wide inference.

questions.prompt: How does unknown differ from any in beginner-friendly terms?

options.text: unknown is identical to any in every way
unknown forces you to narrow before using the value, while any largely disables checking
unknown can only hold numbers
any requires narrowing and unknown never does

questions.explanation: unknown is a safer top type because you must prove more about the value before use.

wrongExplanations.a: They differ in how much checking remains.
wrongExplanations.c: unknown can represent any value until narrowed.

quizzes.title: Checkpoint 2 — Objects, Unions, and Generics
quizzes.intro: Test interfaces, optional fields, unions, narrowing, and lightweight generics.

questions.prompt: What does an interface primarily describe in beginner TypeScript?

options.text: A runtime database connection string
A contract for an object’s shape, such as required properties and their types
A CSS class name
A Git commit message format

questions.explanation: Interfaces document and check object shapes across your program.

wrongExplanations.a: Connection strings are values, not interface definitions.
wrongExplanations.c: CSS is unrelated to TypeScript interfaces.
wrongExplanations.d: Commit messages are process conventions, not TS interfaces.

questions.prompt: What does bio?: string mean on an object type?

options.text: bio must always be provided and must be a string
bio is optional; it may be omitted, and when present it should be a string
bio is a method that deletes strings
bio can only be null, never a string

questions.explanation: The ? marks an optional property that may be missing.

wrongExplanations.c: Optional properties are fields, not delete methods.
wrongExplanations.d: The declared type here is string when present, not only-null.

questions.prompt: Why are string literal unions useful for status fields?

options.text: They allow any random string without feedback
They restrict values to a known set like "draft" | "published" and catch invalid statuses
They replace the need for functions
They only work inside JSON files, not TypeScript

questions.explanation: Literal unions encode allowed states so typos and illegal statuses fail type-checking.

wrongExplanations.a: A plain string allows any text; unions narrow the set.
wrongExplanations.c: Unions complement functions; they do not replace them.
wrongExplanations.d: Unions are a TypeScript type-system feature.

options.text: Deleting unused CSS
Using checks so TypeScript can treat a broader type as a more specific type in a branch
Compressing JavaScript bundles only
Renaming interfaces automatically

questions.explanation: Narrowing refines unions or wide types through typeof checks, equality checks, and similar guards.

wrongExplanations.c: Bundling is a build concern, not type narrowing.
wrongExplanations.d: Renaming is refactoring, not the definition of narrowing.

questions.prompt: What do generics primarily help preserve?

options.text: Runtime encryption keys
Type relationships between inputs and outputs without hard-coding one concrete type
Only CSS color tokens
Git branch names

questions.explanation: Generics keep specificity—for example first<T>(items: T[]) returns T | undefined for whatever T you passed.

wrongExplanations.a: Generics are a type-system tool, not an encryption feature.
wrongExplanations.c: They are not limited to styling tokens.

quizzes.title: Final Quiz — Tooling, Boundaries, and Judgment
quizzes.intro: Apply TypeScript judgment to config mindset, DOM/async boundaries, and common pitfalls.

questions.prompt: Why can casting response.json() as Lesson be risky?

options.text: Because TypeScript assertions validate JSON field-by-field at runtime automatically
Because assertions are compile-time only and do not prove the network payload actually matches Lesson
Because fetch cannot return JSON in browsers
Because Lesson interfaces cannot describe objects

questions.explanation: A cast tells the compiler to trust you; invalid runtime JSON can still arrive.

wrongExplanations.a: Assertions do not perform runtime validation by themselves.
wrongExplanations.c: fetch can return JSON; the issue is trust versus proof.

questions.prompt: What is a practical reason teams enable strict compiler options?

options.text: To make null and implicit any issues harder to ignore so bugs surface earlier
To forbid writing any functions
To replace the need for code reviews
To guarantee zero production incidents forever

questions.explanation: Strict settings catch more incomplete handling—especially around null and implicit any—before runtime.

wrongExplanations.b: You can still write functions; strictness changes checking rules.
wrongExplanations.d: No compiler setting guarantees perfect production outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why might document.querySelector("#save") need careful null handling?

options.text: Because querySelector always throws if the id exists
Because it may return null when the element is missing, and TypeScript models that possibility
Because DOM APIs cannot be used in TypeScript files
Because #save is an invalid CSS selector by definition

questions.explanation: Missing elements yield null; typed DOM APIs push you to handle that case.

wrongExplanations.a: Missing elements typically return null rather than always throwing.
wrongExplanations.c: TypeScript supports DOM typings in browser projects.
wrongExplanations.d: An id selector like #save is normal CSS selector syntax.

questions.prompt: Which approach best matches gradual migration from JavaScript?

options.text: Rewrite every file with advanced generics before shipping anything
Convert files step by step, type important boundaries first, and tighten strictness over time
Delete all tests so types can replace them
Ban interfaces and use only any

questions.explanation: Incremental adoption keeps the product moving while types improve the riskiest contracts first.

wrongExplanations.a: Boiling the ocean stalls teams and is unnecessary for value.
wrongExplanations.c: Types complement tests; they do not fully replace them.
wrongExplanations.d: That removes the benefit of migration.

questions.prompt: When TypeScript shows a cascade of errors after one bad interface field, what should you do first?

options.text: Ignore all messages and add any on every line
Fix the earliest structural issue, then reassess remaining diagnostics
Disable the language service permanently
Convert the file back to CSS

questions.explanation: One root shape mistake often causes many follow-on errors; fixing structure first reduces noise.

wrongExplanations.a: Blanketing any hides the real problem.
wrongExplanations.c: The language service is how you get live feedback.
wrongExplanations.d: CSS is unrelated to repairing type errors.

questions.prompt: A function type-checks and compiles, but users still see wrong data. What does that guarantee?

options.text: Business logic and runtime inputs are necessarily correct
Only that the code is consistent with the declared types—logic, validation, or assumptions may still be wrong
All network payloads were schema-validated
No further testing is ever needed

questions.explanation: Type safety is not proof of correct business behavior or trustworthy external data.

wrongExplanations.c: Compilation does not imply runtime schema validation.
wrongExplanations.d: Tests and product checks remain essential.
